newsitem.title: HONG KONG: HK says won't be hit by Sino-Taiwan shipping ties.
newsitem.headline: HK says won't be hit by Sino-Taiwan shipping ties.

text.p: Hong Kong may lose a slice of its lucrative middleman role if China and Taiwan adopt direct shipping links but the overall impact on the colony would be small, officials and analysts said on Thursday.
"We expect the effect to be rather neutral," said Richard Yuen of the Port Development Board, a government advisory body.

On Wednesday, non-government negotiators from both sides of the Taiwan Strait agreed to allow shipping firms to immediately seek approval to sail between Kaohsiung in Taiwan and Fuzhou and Xiamen in China's Fujian province.

At present, most trade between Taiwan and China passes through third countries, usually Hong Kong, because of Taipei's decades-old ban on direct links with the mainland since the end of the Chinese civil war in 1949.
But analysts said any impact was likely to be small given Hong Kong's location and the sheer size of its port business.
"In 1996, we handled 13.3 million TEUs (20-foot equivalent units of containers), the highest in the world," Yuen told Reuters.
"We estimate that only about one million of the 13.3 million was related to Taiwan-China trade -- that was about eight percent of the total," he said.
Secretary for Economic Services, Stephen Ip, said that while one million containers may be affected, it was premature to predict the real impact.
"It's too early to say how many containers will really be diverted from the Hong Kong route. We'll certainly monitor the development closely," he told reporters.

Yuen said the figure of one million containers bypassing Hong Kong was a worst-case scenario if all China-Taiwan trade stopped going through its port, but explained that was unlikely given Hong Kong's location next to booming southern China.
"From our experience and impression, most of the cargoes going through Hong Kong are from the Pearl River Delta. These cargoes are unlikely to move to ports like Xiamen," he said.
"And on the other hand we think direct shipping links are likely to stimulate Fujian's economic activity, which is good for China and has a positive effect on Hong Kong," Yuen said.
Fujian is on the east China coast across from Taiwan, while the Pearl River Delta is in the south centred around Guangdong Province.
While details of the deal remained murky, the news was enough to drag Hong Kong's benchmark Hang Seng stock market index down 82 points to 13,610 on Thursday.
"People realise that it is not just the physical trade but all the income that goes to the middlemen that we are going to lose," said Janet Gillies, sales director at OCBC Securities."
But even taking the direct shipping links into account, the Port Development Board predicted an eight percent growth in container throughput this year, Yuen said.

"We are likely to lose only about five percent of our total trade," said James Robertson, vice-president at Salomon Brothers. "But this has been developing for some time now and most people have factored it into their equations."
One analyst at a U.S. brokerage said direct shipping links were likely to have the greatest positive impact on Xiamen, which has a good deep-water port.
"The (Chinese) government has wanted to develop that zone for a long time," he added. "In the longer term, this could benefit Hong Kong as the hub of greater China."
